notes: Fast-moving domain: re-check context lines before every release. AI attitudes crossed party lines in 2025-26 polling, so this is a strong cross-cutting candidate.

items.stem: How should the federal government regulate artificial intelligence?
items.scope: Think about AI in general, including chatbots and systems that make decisions about people.
options: Pause development of the most advanced AI until safety rules are in place
Strict rules: testing and approval before major new AI systems are released
Targeted rules for specific harms, like fraud and discrimination, through existing agencies
Few or no new rules; let the industry develop and fix problems as they arise

items.stem: Should states be able to pass their own laws regulating AI?
items.scope: State laws that would apply to AI companies operating in that state.
options: Yes, states should be free to set stricter rules than federal law
Yes, until there is a federal AI law
No; one national standard should override state AI laws
items.notes: Federal preemption of state AI laws was debated in Congress in 2025; watch for answers tracking party positions.

items.stem: How much should competition with China shape US rules on AI?
items.scope: Think about safety rules that could slow US companies down.
options: Not at all; safety rules come first
Somewhat; avoid rules that would put US companies far behind
A lot; staying ahead of China matters more than most safety concerns

items.subtopic: Licensing or testing of the most powerful AI systems
items.stem: Should companies need government approval to release the most powerful AI systems?
items.scope: Only systems far more capable than typical chatbots, built with enormous computing power.
options: Yes, after government safety testing
No approval, but companies must test for dangers and report results to the government
No requirements beyond existing laws

items.subtopic: Licensing or testing of the most powerful AI systems
items.stem: Should companies be allowed to publish their most powerful AI models so anyone can download and change them?
items.scope: Publishing lets researchers inspect the model, and also lets anyone remove its safety limits.
options: No, not the most powerful models
Yes, but only after safety testing
Yes, freely

items.subtopic: Government response to AI job loss
items.stem: If AI replaces many jobs, what should the government mainly do?
items.scope: Assume millions of jobs are affected over 10 years.
options: Slow the use of AI to replace workers
Expand income support, such as cash payments to people who lose work
Fund retraining and help workers find new jobs
Little; new jobs will appear, as with past technology changes

items.subtopic: Government response to AI job loss
items.stem: Should there be legal limits on employers replacing workers with AI?
items.scope: Large employers replacing many workers at once.
options: Yes: require notice and severance, and ban replacing people in some jobs, like teaching and nursing
Require advance notice and severance pay, but no bans
No limits; employers should decide how to use new technology

items.stem: How much should social media companies remove posts that are legal but false or offensive?
items.scope: Think about the largest platforms. This is about what companies choose to do, not what the law requires.
options: Remove much more than they do now
About as much as now
Remove less; leave most legal posts up
Remove only illegal content

items.stem: Should the law limit large social media companies' ability to remove posts or ban users for political views?
items.scope: Platforms with tens of millions of users. Illegal content could always be removed.
options: No; companies should decide what they host
Require them to explain removals and let users appeal
Yes, ban the largest platforms from removing legal political posts

items.stem: Should social media companies be legally responsible for harmful content their users post?
items.scope: Content like defamation or dangerous challenges, not illegal material such as child abuse imagery.
items.context: A 1996 federal law, Section 230, generally shields them from lawsuits over what users post.
options: Yes, for content their systems recommend or promote
Only if they're told about clearly illegal content and don't remove it
No; keep today's protection: users, not platforms, are responsible

facts.claim: 47 U.S.C. sec. 230(c)(1): providers not treated as publisher of third-party content

items.stem: What should the legal minimum age be for having a social media account?
items.scope: Accounts on platforms like Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
options: No legal minimum; parents decide
13, the age most platforms set today

items.stem: Should websites with content for adults only be required to check users' ages?
items.scope: Sites with sexual content or gambling, for example.
options: No; parents should use controls at home
Yes, by methods that don't need ID, like estimating age from a face scan
Yes, with a government ID or similar check

items.stem: Should companies that use AI to screen job or loan applications have to test it for bias against groups such as women or racial minorities?
items.scope: Bias means the system treats equally qualified people differently because of their group.
options: Yes, with independent audits and public results
Yes, companies must test and keep records
No; existing anti-discrimination laws are enough

items.stem: Large data centers for AI use a lot of electricity and water. Which comes closest to your view?
items.scope: Think about new data centers being built across the country.
options: Limit new data centers until there is enough clean power
Allow them, but make them pay the full cost of new power plants and lines
Speed up approval of data centers and power plants to keep the US ahead in AI

items.stem: Should it be illegal to share AI-made fake video or audio of a candidate without labeling it as fake?
items.scope: Realistic fakes meant to look real, not obvious parody.
options: Yes, for anyone sharing it in the months before an election
Only campaigns and paid advertisers must label; no penalties for individuals
No; existing laws against fraud and defamation are enough

items.stem: Should companies pay a special tax when they replace workers with robots or AI?
items.scope: The tax would apply only when a machine takes over work people did.
options: Yes, and use it to support workers who lose jobs
No special tax, but end tax breaks that favor machines over workers
No; it would slow productivity growth
